query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal exposure of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy causes decomposition of the supersaturated matrix and formation of Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates that both act as nucleation sites for a protective MgO-rich scale at high temperatures and create local galvanic cells that change corrosion pathways.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm3) with a homogeneous matrix containing dissolved Mg and early-stage intermetallics.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a defined thermal aging treatment (e.g., heating at an elevated temperature for a set duration) that simulates service or post-processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Temperature high enough to enable microstructural evolution (but below melting), controlled atmosphere for oxidation tests (e.g., air for high-temperature oxidation), and comparison with an untreated control sample.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that emerge during thermal aging.
generation.mechanism: During thermal aging, the supersaturated Mg in the alloy decomposes to form distinct Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates primarily at grain boundaries and within the matrix. At high temperatures, these precipitates oxidize preferentially, forming a continuous, protective, MgO-rich layer that improves oxidation resistance, while their electrochemical potential difference with the surrounding matrix establishes microgalvanic cells that alter corrosion behavior (intensifying localized corrosion in susceptible microregions).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the aged alloy will show improved high-temperature oxidation resistance due to formation of a more uniform protective MgO layer, and concurrently exhibit a change in corrosion patterns (e.g., more localized attack at the intermetallic/matrix interfaces) stemming from the development of galvanic cells.
generation.baseline: The as-cast condition of the alloy, exhibiting a relatively homogeneous distribution of Mg in the matrix with early-stage intermetallic compounds and unoptimized high-temperature oxidation and corrosion properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under the design constraint of lightweight alloys (density <6 g/cm3) with non-equilibrium initial microstructures containing sufficient Mg to drive intermetallic formation under thermal exposure; results might differ with alternative processing techniques or vastly different Mg contents.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of the phase evolution, the exact degree to which the protective MgO scale improves oxidation resistance, and the quantitative impact of galvanic coupling on corrosion rates are not yet fully known and require detailed experimental investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to the specified thermal aging treatment, while keeping the other set as-cast. Characterize the microstructure using microscopy and phase analysis (e.g., TEM, XRD) to detect Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, then perform high-temperature oxidation tests and corrosive environment exposure. Compare the formation of protective oxide scales and corrosion attack patterns between the two sets.
measurements: Microstructural phase identification and quantification of Mg-rich precipitates
Oxide scale continuity and composition (using XRD/EDS)
Corrosion attack mapping and localized corrosion rate measurement (e.g., via electrochemical methods)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal aging treatment does not produce a statistically significant increase in the volume fraction or distinctive distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, or if there is no corresponding improvement in oxidation resistance and alteration of corrosion patterns compared to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.
